analysis.one_liner: Makes it easier for patent owners to get court orders shutting down products found to infringe their patents.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would make court-ordered shutdowns the default in patent cases, sits without action in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, a company found to have infringed a patent does not automatically face a court order to stop; a judge weighs several factors before issuing one, under a 2006 Supreme Court decision. This bill would flip that: once infringement is found, the judge would have to presume an order to stop (a permanent injunction) should be issued, unless the infringing company can show why not. Supporters say this protects small inventors and startups from big companies that copy their inventions and pay damages later; opponents say it hands patent holders a tool to shut down complex products and extract payments.
analysis.who_benefits: Patent owners who win an infringement case would gain a default right to a court order shutting down the infringing product or activity, unless the defendant can show otherwise. The bill's findings single out individual inventors, startups, universities, and small and medium-sized businesses as the intended winners, arguing they currently lack the leverage to stop big companies from copying them. Patent-licensing firms that sue but don't make products would also gain significantly, since injunctions are their strongest negotiating tool.

how_it_helps.text: After a final judgment of infringement, courts would have to presume a permanent injunction should issue, with the losing infringer bearing the burden of showing why not — restoring leverage the Supreme Court took away in eBay v. MercExchange in 2006 [S2].

The bill's findings argue that without an injunction threat, large multinational companies can simply infringe the patents of undercapitalized inventors — individuals, startups, universities, and small businesses — and pay damages later, since money damages come years into a lawsuit and injunctions stop infringement immediately [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies accused of infringement — including large technology and manufacturing firms whose products contain thousands of patented components — would bear the cost of a default risk that their products can be ordered off the market after a single infringement finding, and would spend more fighting injunctions and settling. Consumers could face higher prices or removed products when a court blocks a product rather than letting it continue with a royalty payment.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large product-making companies, and consumers indirectly

drawbacks.text: A company found to infringe a patent could be shut down by court order unless it proves an injunction is unwarranted — a burden that in complex products like smartphones, which contain thousands of patents, could block consumers' access to products over disputes about a single component.

Overturning the 2006 Supreme Court's balancing test in favor of a statutory presumption applies the same rule to every case, including those where a licensing dispute, not a copycat, is really at stake.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem the record itself names — large companies that infringe small inventors' patents because an injunction (and leverage) can't be obtained [S3] — and a default injunction would give those inventors real leverage. But it does so with a blunt rule that applies in every case, not just the ones the findings describe: infringers of all kinds, including those whose products consumers depend on, would face shutdown by default [S3], and the burden shifts to them to prove why an injunction is unwarranted [S2]. A more tailored standard could target willful or continuing infringement without exposing every complex technology product to default shutdown; this bill does not attempt that distinction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 25, 2025 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — has been recorded since the referral, with Congress still in session.
The bill would create a rebuttable presumption favoring permanent injunctions in patent cases, reversing the approach the Supreme Court set in eBay v. MercExchange in 2006.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's position has changed: large companies that infringe patents continue to face damages rather than shutdown orders, and the patent owners who want injunctions do not yet have them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet — the bill sits unacted upon

for.name: Reps. Dean (D-PA), Roy (R-TX), and Johnson (D-GA)
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill at introduction, giving it support from both parties.

for.name: 4 of 217 House Democrats and 2 of 223 House Republicans

sides.party_line_note: The bill's five cosponsors include members of both parties (4 Democrats and 2 Republicans including the sponsor), so it is not a partisan fight so much as an unadopted one — no committee or floor action has occurred [S4].

industries.industry: Patent owners, including non-practicing entities and licensing firms
industries.note: A statutory presumption of an injunction would restore the strongest enforcement tool in patent litigation, making patents more valuable to hold and to assert. This group includes both individual inventors and firms whose business is litigation itself.

Companies that build complex products incorporating many patented technologies would face a default risk of court-ordered shutdown after any infringement finding, raising litigation costs and settlement leverage against them.

industries.industry: Individual inventors, startups, universities, and small and medium-sized enterprises
industries.note: The bill's own findings say these patent holders are the ones most hurt when injunctions are hard to get, because big companies can infringe and pay damages later. A default injunction would give them real leverage.

Brand-name drug makers could more easily block generic or competitor products during patent disputes, which can keep prices higher for consumers; they are also frequent patent plaintiffs, so enforcement leverage cuts both ways.

analysis.trajectory: Similar patent-owner litigation bills have been introduced repeatedly without reaching the floor; referred to Judiciary with no committee activity and no Senate companion momentum, the likely path is that it sits until the Congress ends. A high-profile court fight over patent injunctions or industry backing could revive it, but there is no sign of that in the record so far.
